# Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta (MN 46 (PTS MN i 309))

**ID:** MN 46 (PTS MN i 309)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta  
**PTS:** MN i 309  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul4.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul4.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahādhammasamādāna Sutta* ("The Greater Discourse on Ways of Undertaking Things") is the forty-sixth discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, set at Jeta's Grove near Sāvatthi [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Addressed to the monks, it opens with their affirmation that their teachings have the Blessed One as their source, guide, and resort (*bhagavammūlakā no bhante dhammā bhagavamnettikā bhagavampaṭisaraṇā*) [Marciniak 2019]. Like its companion discourse, the *Cūḷadhammasamādāna Sutta* (MN 45), the sutta expounds four ways of taking up practices or undertaking things, distinguishing them based on whether they are painful or pleasant in the present and whether they ripen in pain or pleasure in the future [Humphreys 1956; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The discourse examines how conduct and views—such as abstaining from or engaging in killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and wrong view—shape one's experiential results and determine future rebirths [Anderson 1999; Rogell 2003].

In the Theravāda commentarial tradition recorded in the *Papañcasūdanī*, the sutta is noted as having been recited at night by a young monk at Paṅgura-vihāra in southern Ceylon (Hatthibhogajanapada), an enchanting recitation that pleased a listening deity (*devatā*) into voicing praise [Adikaram 1946; Rahula 1956].

Curated full parallels to the sutta include two Chinese translations: Madhyama Āgama discourse MĀ 175 and the individual translation T 83 (*Yingfa jing*, 應法經).

**Sources**

- [Adikaram 1946] E. W. Adikaram, Early History of Buddhism in Ceylon (1946) — Records the commentarial tradition of the young monk reciting the sutta at Paṅgura-vihāra.
- [Anderson 1999] Carol S. Anderson, Pain and its Ending: The Four Noble Truths in the Theravada Buddhist Canon (1999) — Discusses the sutta's enumeration of conduct, wrong/right view, and rebirth.
- [Humphreys 1956] Christmas Humphreys (ed.), Buddhist Students Manual (1956) — Summary description of the sutta on the ripening of pleasure and pain.
- [Marciniak 2019] Katarzyna Marciniak, Mahāvastu: A New Edition, Vol. III (2019) — Cites the formula 'bhagavammūlakā no bhante dhammā' at MN i 309.
- [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — English title, setting at Sāvatthi, and doctrinal summary comparing MN 45 and MN 46.
- [Rahula 1956] Walpola Rahula, History of Buddhism in Ceylon: The Anuradhapura Period (1956) — Details the recitation of the sutta at Paṅgura-vihāra and the praise from a deity.
- [Rogell 2003] Sharda Rogell, Pressing Out Pure Honey: A Practitioner's Study Guide (2003) — Describes the sutta's teachings on cause, effect, and wise choices.
